title: Is a fish in the mouth worth two in the water? Some, but not all, beluga whales indicate that it is.
abstract: This essay begins by noting that the adage goes goes, "A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush." Unless you are a beluga whale. Then, neither option is worth much because there are not too many birds, hands, or bushes in your world. But, "a fish in the mouth might be worth two in the water," especially if those two are an unsure prospect in an unsure world. So, what would a beluga whale choose in such a spot, and more importantly, would the choices of one beluga whale align with the choices of another? The study in this issue by M. H. Babb et al. (see record 2027-52608-001) focuses on these questions. The present author concludes that individual differences seem to be the key outcome from this study. The question is what one can learn from those. Babb et al. offered that these could reflect personality traits (something also proposed for the demonstrated individual differences in risk-related decisions in other whale species. With only four individuals in this study, it is hard to make any strong claims, especially when those individuals were all females. That said, individual differences are not merely noise obscuring phenomena of interest. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).
